A correspondent writes us as follows:
Are We Playing the Enemy's Game?
La Sarre, Que.,
Feb. 23, 1942.
Dear Mr. Harvey,
After reading in last week's newspapers the subamendments moved in the House of Commons by Mr. Liguori Lacombe and Mr. Jean Francois Pouliot respectively, it is my opinion that the manifest hypocrisy underlying these amendments is a most disquieting thing for our Freneh-Canadian nation.
And this is the ending of the letter:
This propaganda is certainly of German inspiration and its only object is to create disunity in all allied countries by fostering either racial or religious strife. It seems to perpetuate itself under various forms and I think it is high time our fellow citizens should become aware of the grave danger it presents.
Ldonidas Boisvert
I have only one word to say in this connection and that is that Mr. Jean Charles Harvey's patron saint, Voltaire, had adopted for a motto: "Lie and keep on lying, it is bound to bear some fruit." I might also apply to Messrs. Boisvert and Harvey the following quotation also taken from Voltaire: "Is there enough hellebore for so strange a malady?"
I protest energetically against insinuations of this nature and the only thing left for me to do is to mail a seidlitz powder to Mr. Leonidas Boisvert and the remainder of the

box, to wit eleven powders, to Mr. Jean Charles Harvey who is eleven times sillier than Mr. Boisvert.

speechtext:
It is not my intention to delay the house on this bill; I shall take but a very few minutes. In fact, I had not intended speaking at all on this wheat legislation. As an Ontario member I was willing to accept the government's proposal as drafted in these -bills and let it go at that. Having listened, however, to so much discussion during the last couple of weeks from members on all sides of the house, and more particularly to criticisms that have been made of this legislation by members of the opposition, and having taken part in previous debates on the subject, I feel that as an Ontario farmer I should say a few words.
Since coming to this house about seven years ago I have heard wheat, wheat, wheat for two or three weeks every session. We have talked so much about wheat that we are getting more confused than ever about it. It seems to me that hon. members from the west cannot themselves agree on what they want. The hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) said- the other day that there are two schools of thought in the west so far as wheat policy is concerned. If I am any judge there are more like twenty-two schools of thought. But the difference between the two schools is found in the question whether we should pay so much an acre or so much a bushel. I can understand that for the big farmer who is growing thousands of bushels, so much a bushel may be preferable, but for the man who produces very little, perhaps through crop failure or some such cause, the other proposal is better; and I intend to support the bonus as proposed by the government.
We hear a good deal about this delegation of four hundred farmers that came to Ottawa, the implication being that they have to come here in delegations in order to get any consideration from the government; that they have to come and demand certain things to get anything done. Some of our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends express it by saying that the squeaking wheel gets the grease, the crying baby the milk, and all that sort of thing. I do not believe that is the position at all. I believe the government to-day are doing the very best they can to legislate for the benefit not only of the wheat growers but of all the farmers of Canada. And believe me, it is a big job. The Montreal Financial Times had a good editorial on March 13 in which the comment was made that
"Ottawa boosts wheat price and east must grin and bear it." The editorial goes on to say that the west has been disappointed that the war has not solved the wheat problem. The bonus on coarse grains to encourage mixed farming is a situation full of paradoxes. The paradox is that we are asking the farmers to grow more wheat, and are taking more wheat from the farmers at a higher price, but we cannot sell it. So far as I am concerned I do not think this is anything to grin about, nor would I if I had my own way accept some of the things that have been suggested. But I have agreed to accept the increase in the price of wheat from 70 to 90 cents and the increase from 230 million to 280 millon bushels, for a commodity which at the present time we cannot sell.
The estimated surplus in Canada for this crop year will be 400 million bushels. The United States and the Argentine will have practically another billion bushels, so that there will be a surplus of available wheat of over one and a quarter billion bushels, enough to do us for two or three years if no more were grown. Someone will say of course that if the war should end soon we would have plenty of markets for our wheat. I agree; but it is not very likely that the war will end soon, and the chances are the government is going to have to pay out huge sums of money to carry this wheat until it is needed. I do not say it will not be needed; eventually I believe it will. But I believe the government has gone as far as it should in raising the price, especially in the face of the need for money for armaments, tanks, planes, guns, ships and implements of war. I think the west should be satisfied.
As an eastern farmer when I go home to my constituency or anywhere else in Ontario I hear the old story, "You can't satisfy the west, it makes no difference what you give them. Why don't the farmers of Ontario stand up and oppose this legislation for the west and do something for Ontario?" Well, we are willing to do what we can for the west. We have always taken that attitude. I think hon. members will agree that when I have spoken in this house, on almost every occasion I have upheld the policies submitted to help the west. I have not agreed with everything, but I think I have been at least reasonable. But our farmers say, "If you give the western farmers 90 cents for wheat, they want a dollar; if they are given a dollar, they want $1.25." That is the attitude the farmers of Ontario take to-day. All the farmers are bonused

 we quite agree with that-not only in the
Wheat Board Act

west but in the whole of Canada. The government is spending from the end of July, 1941, to August 1, 1942, over $84 million on bonuses to farmers, of which over $62 million goes to the west. We have bonused coarse grains at $2 an acre, grass at $2 am acre, summer-fallow at $2 an acre-all these things. It makes the Ontario resident, not only the farmer but all Ontario citizens, wonder what we are doing or where we are going with this legislation. A new price is set for wheat, and there is some justification for it; but people compare that with the deficit of the Canadian National Railways, $50 million a year in recent years, and it is suggested that this wheat policy may cost the government $130 million. I am not going to argue whether that is right or wrong. I do not think anyone knows what it is going to cost, but I believe it will cost an enormous sum, considerably over the $50 million deficit of the Canadian National Railways in recent years.
The other day the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) said he thought the Ontario fanners were willing to accept dollar wheat; that they would accept anything that was reasonable if the west proposed it. I say right here that we are not accepting dollar wheat, and we are not accepting whatever the west proposes. We have problems of our own in Ontario; the west is not the only place that has a farm problem. We have the tobacco growers, the bean growers and others whose problems have been discussed1 by other hon. members-

Yes, they have had no assistance of any account in Ontario. It has cost the government of this country very little for Ontario. Most of it has gone to the west and the east.
I have every sympathy for the west. I have visited the west; I have been all through the burnt-out areas in southern Saskatchewan, and I know the condition the people were in when I was there. I have every sympathy for them, and I am willing, as I said before, to support any legislation within reason to help them. But as Ontario members we cannot hand out everything to the west. Someone has said that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is from the west and therefore is naturally sympathetic with the western farmer. But I believe that the Minister of Agriculture to-day is doing the very best he can for all the farmers and all the people of Canada, regardless of east or west. More than that, I believe that in this measure he is trying to legislate for the small farmer more than for the man who has 10,000 or 20,000 or 50,000 or 100,000

bushels of wheat. This legislation will help the small farmer, and we are willing to accept it.
Someone has said, what about coarse grains? Well, it has cost the government about $6,000,000 for freight to bring coarse grains down to Ontario. Ontario farmers were glad to get them, yet many hon. members speaking here were opposed to the coarse grain provision. As it happened, this year we were short of feed in Ontario, and many farmers were glad to get coarse grain to feed hogs and cattle and to produce milk, butter and eggs. But those are things that are in demand; those are things we can sell. That is not the case with wheat. The farmers have played a very important part in this war effort, and I know they will continue to do so. The farmers are willing to contribute everything they have toward winning the war. If perhaps they do not get parity prices, they are willing to go on anyway; and I believe the west should adopt the same attitude. We do hope, however, to hoar some expression of satisfaction from some section of the west. I predict that if this sort of thing goes on very much longer Ontario may become the depressed province, instead of Saskatchewan, because certainly the west is getting all the legislation for its benefit.
I am not going to take up any more time, Mr. Speaker. As I said at the outset, I had not intended to speak on this question; I had made up my mind to accept the proposals of the government. These bills are to be referred to a committee, where I think all bills concerning agricultural policy should be sent. There we will have ample opportunity to discuss every phase of these bills and, I hope, arrive at some decision that will be beneficial to the farmers of Canada as a whole. May I add that I intend to oppose the amendment and to vote for the main motion.

Mr. Speaker, since I am a member of the agriculture committee, to which these various bills are being referred, and since any changes to be made will in all probability be made during that stage of the proceedings, my remarks will be brief.
In passing I should like to make reference to some of the statements of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Rickard). I have no intention of entering into any controversy as between east and west; I deplore it when hon. members feel it necessary to raise that issue in this house. I must say to the hon. member, however, that if this agricultural policy for western Canada is costing eastern Canada money, let eastern Canada remember that from 1932 down to the present

Wheat Board Act
time we in the west have been penalized to the extent of around $90,000,000 a year in order to uphold the tariff and fiscal policies of the east. This year we are getting back just a little of what we have given eastern Canada.
So far as the amendment is concerned, I should think all hon. members of this house who have at heart the welfare of agriculture should support it. I am sorry that the majority of western Liberal members apparently feel obliged to vote against it because, as most of them have stated, of political reasons. I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) for having the courage of his convictions. This is not the first time he has found it necessary to vote against government measures in this house, and I am sure the people of his constituency must appreciate the fact that they are represented by a member who has sufficient courage to vote against the government when he feels they are not promoting the general welfare of the country.
Western people will very much regret the fact that this government has not seen fit to adopt the recommendations of the various farm organizations of this country who have asked for parity prices. The lowest price that has been submitted by any of these organizations I think is SI per bushel. I remember that last year the Minister of Agriculture stated no farm organization had said what it considered to be a fair price. That is not the case this year. The lowest price mentioned was $1 per bushel, while some of the organizations asked for more. The price being paid the farmers of the United States is considerably higher than that, about $1.27, and the price that was paid the farmers of Australia back in 1940 also was considerably higher than the price we received then or will receive under this proposal. In 1940 the farmers of Australia received 3 shillings 6 pence a bushel at point of delivery. I know the Minister of Agriculture has said that this amounts to only 63 cents in Canadian funds, but the Australian farmers are not paid in Canadian funds. They are paid in Australian funds, and in Australia three and six is worth 84 cents. That will buy 84 cents' worth of Australian goods; it will pay 84 cents' worth of Australian taxes, and 84 cents' worth of Australian debt. The farmers of that country are not interested in whether or not that will buy only 63 cents' worth of Canadian goods. The price being paid in Australia to-day is three shillings per bushel, which is 73 cents in Australian funds; and again I use Australian rather than Canadian funds. It is true that 44561-87
in Canadian funds that is only 53 cents, but they are receiving not Canadian but Australian currency, in which it is equivalent to 73 cents a bushel.
It is up to the government to decide to what extent it is necessary to restrict the purchases of wheat. But in that regard we must keep in mind the fact that it is very necessary and essential to the welfare of the country that ample reserves of all kinds of foodstuffs shall be maintained wherever possible, so that when the enemy is driven out of the occupied countries those vast supplies may be made available to the people of those countries. That can be held out to them now to show what can be done. The last hon. member who spoke deplored the fact that we were building up these reserves. We should glory in the fact that we are able to do so, because that will be the greatest incentive to these occupied areas to hold out. While it is up to the government to decide to what extent purchases shall be restricted, I should say it is not up to the government to decide whether or not the farmers shall receive a parity price. I say that because it is a very direct obligation on this government to see that the farmers shall receive a parity price. Otherwise they will brand themselves as a bunch of hypocrites. All this talk about a new social order will become just so much blather. Of what use is it to subscribe to the declaration of principles known as the Atlantic charter unless we are prepared to put those same principles into operation within our own country? How can we hope to solve the problems of the world if we cannot even solve our own problems? Surely the first thing to do is to put our own house in order.
Several hon. members have referred to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture at page 1211 of Hansard, as follows:
We are taking every last dollar out of the treasury of Canada to deal with these problems which we feel it is safe to take at this present time.
That does not mean, of course, that the amount of money being made available for agriculture is all the money the government can get. The government can get all the money it needs for anything. That is not the point, and 1 do not think that was what the minister meant. I believe the minister meant that this was all the money the government could safely put into circulation without the danger of inflation. In other words, if they paid the farmers more than 90 cents a bushel at this time it would create such an effective demand against our production that it would divert a certain amount of goods from the war effort into channels of consumption. The

Wheat Board Act

government should be in the best position to know whether that argument is sound. Nevertheless, even if that statement be correct, the farmers still are entitled to a parity price. You could either reduce the prices of all commodities down to the level of wheat, or on the other hand you could increase the price of wheat so that it would be in line with the prices of other commodities. If there is a danger that by increasing the price of wheat we might bring about inflation in this country, then I would suggest to the government that the most logical way to take care of that question, in order that the farmer shall receive a parity price, would be to make up the difference between 90 cents a bushel and the parity price by an issue to the farmer of war savings certificates maturing after the war, so that such war savings certificates could not be used for present day consumption. This would provide a sinking fund to take care of any increase in a farmer's debts.

It all depends upon what parity is based on. If parity is based on the 1913-14 level it will be different from the 1926 level. I d'o not believe the farmer would quarrel if we were to take the price of $1.20 a bushel, a price which has been stated by many organizations as a necessary one. The establishment of a parity price could easily be found out by reference to records in the bureau of statistics.
The minister has repeatedly stressed the point that a higher price for wheat does not help the man who does not raise wheat owing to a crop failure. Unfortunately the minister insists, I will not say deliberately-I do not know-upon confusing two entirely different problems, namely, the problem of a distressed industry and that of a distressed area. These are separate problems, and if the minister tries to deal with them as one he will bring greater confusion that we have had in the past.
The first of these, namely, a distressed industry-in this instance wheat growing-can be met only by paying the wheat growers a price based on the average cost of production. Some hon. members say, "What is the cost
[Mr. Quelch.l
of raising wheat when you get only two bushels to an acre?" Well, any hon. member may try to offer an absurd argument, but when he uses an argument of that kind I suggest he is making himself absurd, not the argument. In such circumstances the cost of production would be based upon the average yield. If any land consistently produced wheat at a very low yield, it would naturally have to be taken out of production. Such a price would be based upon the average. As I said to the hon. member who interrupted me a moment ago, the price to the farmer should be commensurate with the price he pays for other commodities.
It is not necessary for me to quote statistics to prove these facts. So many statistics have already been put on record that if one were to attempt to read them it would make him dizzy. What will be the result if we fail to pay the farmer a price based upon the cost of production? We know that in the past fifteen years or so farmers have certainly had to accept prices much below that, with the result that a very large percentage of agriculture is to-day in a state of bankruptcy. We have built up tremendous debts. If we are going to continue to pay the farmer a price which is still below the cost of production, not only will he not be able to pay the debts he incurred in the past, but he will still further increase his current debts.
A few months ago I listened to a broadcast by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in which he urged farmers to put their farms on a sound basis and to pay off the debts they had incurred in the past. The wheat growers of Canada will not be in a position to do that unless they receive a price at least equivalent to the cost of production. And, mind you, that will meet only current costs; even that price will not make it possible for them to pay their past debts.
The minister has suggested that the bonus increases the price of wheat by 30 cents a bushel. That sounds all right if you _ can make people believe it; but we know it is a nonsensical argument, because only one of the three bonuses can in any shape or form be regarded as an increase in the price of wheat. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act merely takes care of low yield. After the amendment now on the order paper is passed a farmer will be able to get a bonus only if he raises less than eight bushels to the acre. In Alberta the average yield is eighteen bushels per acre. So that the majority of farmers will not benefit under that bonus and therefore will not receive any increase in price.

Wheat Board Act
Next we have the wheat acreage reduction plan, which merely compensates the farmer for lost acreage. In the district in which I reside the land is of gumbo quality, and many of the farmers crop their land every year. Someone may say that that is wheat mining, that the land can only stand that for a limited number of years. Nevertheless that is the practice on that gumbo land, and they get good crops nearly every year. If they take a certain amount of land out of production to get the bonus, that bonus does not begin to compensate them for the loss in production of wheat, and it cannot possibly be considered as an increase in the price of all the wheat they raise.
The only bonus which in any shape or form may be considered as an increase in price for wheat, is the bonus of 75 cents, and that amounts to only a few cents a bushel. I insist therefore that the only way to take care of a distressed industry is by giving it a parity price. No bonus as paid to-day will take care of that situation.
I should like now to deal with distressed areas. The most logical way to deal with distressed areas would be by some form of crop insurance. It is true that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a step in that direction. Hon. members in this group have consistently supported that measure, although we tried to amend it in certain respects. The fact remains however that the principle of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has always had our support. It is a very long way, however, from being satisfactory, and will still be unsatisfactory even if the amendment now before the agriculture committee is adopted.
For example, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does not guarantee to the farmer, who may pay into that fund for twenty years, that if he has a crop failure he will get a single cent of compensation. That condition arises because the settlement is not on the individual basis, but rather on a township basis. The minister objects to the individual basis on the ground that it would in effect be subsidizing inefficiency. I believe that could, easily be taken care of if we had a sound form of administration. Thoughout the west committee men should be elected by the farmers in each district to take care of the regulations under this measure. Unfortunately the men who are sent around as inspectors to-day apparently are appointed chiefly on the grounds of their political faith. I believe that is a fair statement; I know it is certainly true in my part of the country. About the only qualification a man has to have in order to be an inspector is to be a good Liberal, and to my mind that has been
one of the chief weaknesses of the policies of the Minister of Agriculture in the past. Everything has been regarded by him from a political angle. Every opportunity has been taken to build up a political organization instead of developing a policy which would be of great value to the nation. I am not surprised that the prairie farm assistance organization has bogged down in Alberta- and it certainly has bogged down. Every hon. member from that province is receiving numbers of letters from farmers who say that in their localities there are still many who have not received their payments. The result of having this type of inspector has been the building up of a great deal of antagonism between the farmers and the inspectors, where a healthy spirit of cooperation should exist.
I know the minister is not pleased when we make comparisons between what is being done in Canada and in other countries. He upbraided the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) when he referred to the policy of the AAA. I should like however to quote from an address made by Mr. Evans, the administrator, before the national AAA conference at Washington in 1941. I suggest to the minister that instead of objecting to statements of this kind he should seek to find in them anything that is good in the administrations of other countries and see if it could not be helpful in solving the problems of this country. By way of drawing a comparison between the administration in the United States and the administration in this country, I quote from page 2 of this report as follows:
Now, what are our assets? First, we have an administrative organization that deals directly and personally with more than six million farm families. It is an effective organization whose steadily increasing efficiency demonstrates on a grand scale that you can have democracy and efficiency too.
He puts that as the first asset under the AAA, this democratic organization.
Second, we have the goodwill and respect of the bulk of farmers and of a considerable portion of the leaders of the people. True, we have made some enemies but we have made more friends. Strong friends and strong enemies are a mark of strength. Third, with the assistance of AAA and cooperating agencies, farmers are the best informed large group in America on national and international affairs. Fourth, we have the first large-scale example of a working economic democracy in the world. By economic democracy, I mean the right and the means whereby the individual has an opportunity to share in decisions which affect his economic welfare.
I am not suggesting that we have this condition in the west as the result of the policy
Wheat Board Act

of the Minister of Agriculture; all we have is a large political organization. On page 6 of the pamphlet in which the speech of Mr. Evans, the administrator of the AAA, is printed under date of January 29, 1942, appears the following:
In every county and community, our programme is run by farmer committee men elected by their neighbours. From the ranks of these
130,000	committee men, our state committees are appointed by the secretary of agriculture. Many of the men in administrative, policy forming positions in our department of agriculture are farmers who have come up through the ranks of our farm programme in these past eight or nine years.
For the nation, this investment in farm democracy is already paying dividends. Our whole farm production is now being geared to meet the increased needs of war-food for freedom, we call it-for ourselves and our allies.
Since last spring we have been operating on a basis of selective production.
Last April the secretary of agriculture called for an immediate expansion in hogs, dairy products, poultry, eggs and certain vegetables to meet our rising needs at home and for shipment to Great Britain. Later other commodities, such as soybeans and peanuts for oil, were added. Certain provisions of our programme were modified to encourage these increases. 130,000 AAA farmer committee men went to work to secure the needed production.
Another weakness of the Prairie Farm Assistance Aot is the fact that the returns to the farmer are altogether too low. Suppose we were to pay the farmer $1 for his wheat and then institute a system of crop insurance; if it were upon a blanket basis the farmer would not object in the least to paying as much as 5 per cent instead of the 1 per cent he pays at present in order to have a real crop insurance scheme.- The Minister of Agriculture summarily dismisses the idea of crop insurance by saying that it would be ultra vires of the dominion. He knows that if the government of this country were really in favour of instituting a form of crop insurance they could overcome any constitutional difficulty. This is what happened in the case of unemployment insurance. They could cooperate with the provinces in order to get the necessary amendments put through.
I think it would be well to place on Hansard a brief summary of the crop insurance plan in operation to-day in the United States. This appeared in the Calgary Herald in February- I have forgotten ithe exact date. It reads as follows:
1.	Farmers may insure either 50 or 75 per cent of their average yield against unavoidable hazards (not against neglect).
2.	Insurance is written in terms of bushels. If a grower suffers loss he is entitled to receive from the reserve an indemnity which in terms of bushels is sufficient to bring his yield up to the insured amount.

3.	Average yield is determined separately for each farm on the basis of its actual or approved yield history during the nine year base period covering 1930-38.
4.	Premium rate is calculated separately for each farm.
5.	County AAA committees calculated insurable yields and premium rates for all wheat farms.
6.	Premium may he paid in warehouse receipts, cash or by executing an advance against future payments to be earned under AAA programmes.
7.	To obtain insurance the grower fills out an application containing the information as to his intended plantings and pays the amount of wheat specified for premiums.
Of course if such a programme were adopted in Canada wheat could be turned over to the farmer to indemnify him for his loss, and that wheat would be turned in under his quota as set by the wheat board. I do hope the government will carefully consider this matter of crop insurance. The antagonism that exists in eastern Canada would be largely overcome if we could introduce some form of contributory crop insurance. I am not suggesting for one minute that you could obtain from the farmers enough to finance the plan, but you would at least have a plan under which every farmer who suffers loss would get some form of compensation, without any increase in cost to the federal treasury.
In closing I should like to make a few remarks about our general agricultural policy. For a number of years we have urged in this house that a long-term programme should be adopted, based upon international cooperation instead of international competition. We know that international competition can lead to one thing and one thing only, that is, international Motion which leads to war. Furthermore, we must realize that it is useless for Canada to act alone. Last year Canada was able to bring about a substantial reduction in wheat production, but what happened? The other three major exporting nations increased their surpluses, so that in so far as the world surplus was concerned we were no beter off. This should be done on an international basis.
I remember the Minister of Agriculture telling the United Farmers of Alberta in January of last year that they should not increase their production of hogs, and yet within six months of that time we were told that we might have to ration our bacon and pork products.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on wheat is a hardy annual. Ever since I can remember, it has been one of the most important topics that has been before the house and dealt with bj' parliament. I must say that the legislation brought down in this bill, No. 13, is the most attenuated form of legislation dealing with wheat that I have ever seen. I shall have something to say about that a little later, when I come to refer to the orders in council which were passed about the time the minister moved the second reading of this bill.
It is a matter of some satisfaction to me to know that the policy of establishing a wheat board laid down and put into effect in 1935 by the government of which I was a member is, in its broad aspects, the basis of the policy under which the present government has been operating since this war began. And this notwithstanding the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1935, when, afraid to make a frontal attack, they under the leadership and direction of the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), then the financial critic of the opposition, made every kind of flank attack it was possible to make. What followed is a matter of history. I referred in the speech which I made on the first day of August, 1940, on the second reading of the bill then before the house to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to the disasters which followed the ineptitude of government policy, especially in relation to the handling of the 1938-39 wheat crop, when the treasury and the farmers of Canada suffered severe loss, and to the fire sale of good Canadian wheat held at the instance of the govern-
Wheat Board Act

ment, when we sustained a loss of millions of dollars which might and should have been avoided.
Time is a great healer, and in the position we occupy to-day it has brought about some vindication of the position taken in 1935. I desire only at this time to refer to the advice I then gave the government, that "not one kernel of this wheat should be destroyed. It may be needed by suffering humanity before this war is over."
In his speech on the second reading of this bill the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) emphasized the difficulties encountered over a period of ten years by the dominion government in dealing with this problem. This proves that the problem is not primarily a war problem but one of long Standing. He laid down the principle that it was possible to decide upon each year's programme only after weighing all factors capable of measurement or accurate appraisal. This means that the government believes it is not possible to lay down a wheat policy for the duration of the war. From that view I respectfully dissent.
It seems to me that if we are to know where we are going, if our wheat producers are to plan intelligently, instead of awaiting anxiously each year an announcement of government policy, the government should if possible lay down a policy visualizing the war period, with no very material changes as regards marketing abroad in sight. This in order that the wheat producers, the persons most affected materially, may be in a position to know what they can count on, what they can do, and then can plan accordingly-that is, if they are to continue producing wheat, even with production reduced. We now know all the factors except the volume of the new crop each year, and the duration of the war.
Just at this point and in this connection, there would appear to me to be one fundamental consideration. During the period of the war the purchase of 2S0 million bushels annually would appear to be an economic necessity if the farmers of the west are not to be compelled to go on relief. If in any year the surplus on hand at the end of the crop year falls below the amount of 400 million bushels, additional wheat could be bought to bring the surplus up to that figure. But any quantity over and above the amount of 280 million bushels should be produced only at the risk of the producer and without obligation on the part of the board to purchase.
Frankly I think the minister will find that the farmer is not satisfied with the price of 90 cents f.o.b. Fort William. It is a compro-

mise. The price structure thus established is not to be confused with grants under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which are in an entirely different category and made on a different principle. The established price does not bear any relation to the grants under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act except in one respect, that is, the gross income of the prairie farmer.
Before entering upon a general discussion of the bill I should like to make some reference to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on the tenth instant, arising out of the amendment to the bill proposed by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and now before the house.
The minister, with his usual adroitness, attempted to show that in every line of major agricultural production except wheat there exists to-day parity of prices. That may be true in part, but if so, it is only of very recent occurrence and was not true either in whole or even in part a year ago. It was not true in April, 1941, when the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved his resolution for parity of prices on a motion of the Minister of Finance to go into supply. On that occasion every member of this house supporting the Liberal party voted against the principle of parity prices, a principle which the minister now seeks to convince the house is the policy of this government. But with respect to wheat, the minister had no case, and admitted it. In fact, he said there was no parity but that the price would be brought up to parity as soon as financial conditions warranted. Having regard to the way in which the government has wasted money on certain activities-one and a quarter million dollars for the plebiscite, and others I could mention-it occurs to me that the minister's plea for delay was entirely beside the mark.
The minister is a past master at special pleading. His defence against the amendment was in effect what we old common law lawyers call a plea of confession and avoidance. He admits the allegation in the declaration and then seeks to avoid the consequences by suggesting that we wait and see what will happen another session. It was clever, but to me it was not convincing. The minister made much of the assistance rendered to the western farmer under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and sought to convey the impression that the grants under that act were in effect an additional price for wheat to the producer. I do not so interpret the principle of that act. It is in my view in essence a relief measure. We have not opposed that principle, but we

Wheat Board Act
have endeavoured to show that the cost of administration is abnormally high, that the staff constitutes a huge political machine, and in its incidence it is inequitable.
I suggest to the minister that the true principle upon which it should operate is that individual necessity resulting from loss of crop, compensated for by the act, should be cared for on the basis of each individual need rather than by blanket legislation administered by a political machine. The result has been that considerable payments have been made to individuals who should be carrying themselves instead of drawing upon public funds needed for war purposes. I am informed that this legislation gives public money to some individual farmers who are in a position to carry on out of their own resources. The same applies in some instances to the provisions of last year's grants for summer-fallow, under which some large farm operators have been paid for following farming practices which good husbandry requires that they should do anyway and which they are well able to do.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) predicated his remarks on five major factors which he said had to be considered. He itemized these on March 9 on page 1120 of Hansard. Some of them are of major importance and some are not. He dealt with the carryover, the well-being of the economy of the prairie provinces as well as of Canada as a whole, the extent to which the dominion government could act in respect of the wheat problem, without detracting from our immediate objectives in respect of the war -this is always a cloak of government policy- and then export markets, and so on. There is a further major consideration to which the minister did not refer, and it is this: that in arriving at a decision to raise the initial price from 70 to 90 cents, regard had to be given to the policy of the government with respect to the maintenance of the price ceiling structure.
That you cannot have your cake and eat it too is a trite saying, but the principle is involved in this matter. I can imagine the controversy in the cabinet between those who wanted to maintain the price ceiling structure on, say, bread, and those who, for various reasons, both economic and political, advocated a higher price for wheat. In this connection may I refer to an article sent out by the Star syndicate early this month to certain newspapers across Canada., in which the following appears:
On the one hand Hon. J. G. Gardiner and the block of 15 Liberal Saskatchewan members have been exerting pressure on the government which savors of an ultimatum. It is known that the Saskatchewan members have discussed
crossing the floor of the Commons to the opposition benches and that word of this probability has been communicated to the cabinet.
On the other hand, determined to maintain the price ceiling, Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices board, is standing firmly against any boost in price of wheat just now. There has been talk of Mr. Gardiner resigning unless something is done, and of Mr. Gordon relinquishing his post if the prairie demand is met.
I shall not comment further.
It should be distinctly understood that a policy of a parity price for wheat should be for the duration of the war only and for a reasonable time thereafter. When that time comes, the whole policy should be thoroughly reviewed and overhauled. This country, an agricultural country, cannot go on indefinitely with a bonus policy. It is uneconomic and unsound, and, in the minds of many thoughtful agriculturists, would be doing a distinct disservice to agriculture itself.
To-day there are many forms of agriculture which are receiving no assistance whatever. I instance the potato industry in my own province, which has not received any assistance and Which has passed through a very trying time in recent years.
The picture painted by the minister of our carryover is not too bright. As at February 1, according to information which I have from the Monthly Wheat Review, the visible supply available for export was 535 million bushels. What is the estimate of export from now till the end of the crop year? Twenty million bushels per month? This is very doubtful in view of the submarine menace. The Canadian carryover may reach 450 million bushels. Certainly it will not be less than 400 million bushels. The United States carryover is estimated at not less than 600 million bushels, and it may be more. The United States and Canada together will have at least 1,050 million bushels between them, and perhaps much more. The Argentine and Australia have a carryover of from 300 million to 400 million bushels, or a grand total of say 1,400 million bushels as a minimum.
I suggest to the house and to the country that that is not an attractive outlook for the immediate future having regard to the severe restrictions on export and lack of available markets. Notwithstanding all this I think it is the part of wisdom that Canada should continue to produce wheat in such quantities as will ensure a reservoir of food for domestic purposes, for use by the people of Britain and against the time which will surely come when it will be required for the starving peoples of Europe, provided of course-and I put in this proviso-that the surplus in this country should1 not exceed that now on hand.
Wheat Board Act

In this connection may I ask the Minister of Agriculture and his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce if they and the government have been exploring the possibility of contributing to a general international reservoir of food supplies? This question was raised recently by the Vice-President of the United States, Mr. Henry A. Wallace, himself an authority, and it is well he did so; for a general reservoir of foodstuffs is going to be required in this war-ridden world, and in such a reservoir there is no one commodity of more general or better use than wheat.
In considering this question of carryover it must be borne in mind that both the United States and Canada will, by August next, have new harvests on their hands; and that is an important factor. The western farmer is prepared to reduce his wheat acreage provided he is paid an economic price for his products. But with reduced production he must have an economic return for what he does produce.
I suggest further that it is sound economic policy that the western farmer should not produce more than can be marketed for export and domestic consumption. But if he is to be kept on the land he must be paid a price that will permit him to maintain himself, and 90 cents, with reduced production and with quota restrictions, would appear to me to be too low. And mark this: the farmer's costs have been going up and will go up all the time, price ceiling or no price ceiling, and the labour shortage at the next harvest will again increase his costs.
We in this house should also realize that the real wheat area in western Canada is not suitable for mixed farming-at least I have come to that conclusion after having seen it -and that there are large areas in the west which must depend on wheat and wheat alone.
I am prepared to accept that position; I think Canada should accept it. To me it appears almost wicked to reduce production of first class foodstuffs when it is known that so many millions are starving and will starve before this long war is over.
These are two points of view. But we must be realistic. We know that our production cannot be delivered to these starving millions. We must also be realistic, knowing that the war has not been the cause of these carryovers. We had them long before the war; they are attributable in part to pre-war economic policies of continental Europe and in part to the ineptitude of this government in handling the problem in the years immediately preceding the war. Even if peace had prevailed we should have had an enormous surplus of wheat in Canada. The war did not cause the wheat problem of 1938 or 1939; we had it then because of the policy of this tMr. R. B. Hanson,]
country at that time, or rather the lack of any realistic policy. Therefore I think we should decide to carry the surplus now in sight, but should not permit it to increase beyond its present or anticipated level; and we should have some control of production and a higher price for what is needed for home use and export.
When the wheat board was set up in 1935 the initial price was fixed by the Bennett government at 87i cents a bushel f.o.b. Fort William. We are only now approaching that price; and that was at a time when the cost of production was much less than it is to-day. The 1942 crop may be below normal, and we may be able to afford to take some chances on a decrease rather than have an increase above our present load of carryover. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) referred to that possibility yesterday, judging from moisture conditions in the west last fall. That may be. We may be able to gamble something on that. But this country should decide to produce only sufficient for domestic use plus a reasonable amount for export, which the minister and the government have placed at 280 million bushels, if I understand it correctly. In any event this year's crop should not exceed 300 million bushels; that would appear to be ample and more than ample.
Here I pause to ask the minister, in connection with the export trade, whether he is aware that the United Kingdom are taking steps to increase production on their own soil this year, and whether he is aware, as of course he must be, that the government of the United Kingdom is taking steps to decrease the consumption of wheat flour? These are matters which cannot be ignored.
I pass now to another subject. We should, not visualize a policy of production of wheat in order that it may be fed to hogs, because barley and oats are a cheaper crop and a more satisfactory feed. In passing I should like to raise another question which I believe is giving some concern in certain quarters.
I ask the ministers, what has been done by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce about conserving seed barley and seed oats? It has been reported to me that a dominion government representative visited the prairie provinces at least three months ago to inquire into the position of seed barley and oats; it is understood that these seeds are scarce, and nothing appears to have been done about it. Perhaps the ministers will enlighten us on that point.
I offer this suggestion. The acreage of these feed grains should be increased to

Wheat Board Act
offset the reduction in wheat acreage. The policy enunciated by the Minister of Agriculture would appear to encompass that policy. The only solution from the standpoint of the western farmer therefore seems to be to reduce the wheat acreage materially and increase the acreage of oats and barley. This involves the payment to the wheat farmer of a sufficiently high price to give him a fair return, and it is represented to me that at least $1 at the country elevators would not be any more than ample.
Encourage increased acreage of barley and oats, and build up farm stocks of these feeds in order to increase, within reasonable limits, hog and dairy production. These, as well as wheat, are the foods that the millions suffering and dying from malnutrition will want as soon as possible after the sea lanes are opened. People in starving Europe cannot live on starch alone. They have to have other foods as well.
The weakness of the present policy is that it is not based on any long term plan. It is a piecemeal policy. That seeems to have been the position ever since the war began. If you visualize the 1940 policy, the 1941 policy and now this 1942 policy you will see it is and has been merely a piecemeal policy, not based on any general principle but designed to meet only a temporary situation and to yield, grudgingly though it may be, to the demands of the western wheat farmer. My understanding is that the government's firm policy was to fix the price at 70 cents plus a bonus, and that, as I understand it, would have been in conformity with the price ceiling policy.
The wheat farmer, I am told, does not like the bonus. He looks upon it as a handout or charity, and as he is a self-respecting man no one can blame him. He wants, and rightly so, something like a parity price for his product. He wants to be treated as nearly as may be on the same principle as labour and industry are being treated by the government during this war. But, I ask you, is he? I think the answer is obvious. There is ample evidence in the proceedings of this parliament alone that the government's policy was a low initial price plus a bonus.
How can the government pay the farmer $1 or even 90 cents for wheat and maintain the price ceiling? I put that question to the minister. The answer would appear to be that it cannot be done without either raising the price of bread or handing out a bonus to someone on the way down, either the miller or the baker. Apparently the government, being on the horns of a
44561-S8
dilemma, has chosen the latter course. When the Prime Minister announced the price ceiling policy last autumn with such a flourish of trumpets it was stated definitely that it would be maintained at all costs. The price ceiling was announced at a time when the price level was uneven, especially so with respect to wheat and certain other farm products.
I know it was so with respect to the farm products of New Brunswick, potatoes and hay. A ceiling was put on hay based on the price between a certain date in September and a certain date in October, just after the new crop had come in, when every year so far as I can remember hay is at its lowest peak. Was that fair to the hay farmers of the Saint John valley? No attempt was made to arrive at a fair and uniform price structure before the plan was put into effect. This left so many inequalities that every month since the Prime Minister made his announcement there have been alterations in the ceiling, generally upward.
What does this mean? It means that the whole scheme has been a system of trial and error, not based on any principle. It was announced as a means of preventing inflation. Well and good; but its effect has been to freeze wages, with the cost of living bonus a sop to labour. The people who had to suffer most were the primary producers, and in particular the producers of foodstuffs, of whom the chief was the wheat farmer. He has been the chief sufferer.
I raise this question at this point: Was any consideration given to the price of wheat when the ceiling price policy was put into effect last autumn; and if not, why not?

speechtext: The Prime Minister said so, in his statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Well, then, what consideration was given to it? They did not fix a fair even price. In the struggle to prevent inflation, in the attempt to freeze wages, why was not consideration given in setting up this national price plan to fixing a parity price for wheat, or something approaching a parity price? It could have been done much more easily then than now. Had it been done at that time I am convinced that the western farmer would have had $1 wheat, and there would have been no great storm over it in eastern Canada, either. It would have been relatively easy to do it then, and the consequent adjustments could have been made without any great disturbance. But the mechanics of the situation have been reversed, in an effort to get what the western farmer thinks is only justice,
REVIftEB EDITION
Wheat Board Act

having regard to the position of the wage-earners and industrialists of Canada. That was one reason why the Saskatchewan farmers came to Ottawa early this session and presented their case. I have never understood, Mr. Speaker, the criticism that has been directed from some quarters against those gentlemen coming down to Ottawa on that pilgrimage. As I view it, their whole future is at stake, and surely it is their right to carry their grievances to the foot of the throne, like any other subject.
It must be borne in mind that while the price of 90 cents for wheat announced by the minister represents a floor, it is in effect a ceiling too. The farmers of western Canada should not be led to expect very much spread between this floor and a ceiling; in my view there is no spread at all. You cannot operate a national price structure such as we are attempting to operate in Canada, and leave certain important commodities, such as wheat, to run wild. If there is much likelihood of an upward trend in the open market, what will happen? The grain exchange will have to be closed, as it was in the last war. This statement, of course, is predicated upon the assumption that a rigid price structure is to prevail.
Now, presumptuous as it may seem, I have a word to say to all the farmers of Canada, and it is this: that in this war period they should1 avail themselves of the opportunity to inform themselves fully with respect to a national price plan and what its effect is and will be upon them. I assert that they are now pinned under such a plan. The basis and objective of that plan at the moment is to help beat Hitler. But if we are to have a planned economy after the war; if we are to have a national plan fixing prices, such as our friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are urging should be put into effect after the war, is it not likely that among the problems, all much less urgent than the war, the most pressing and urgent would be those of employment in large centres and problems arising out of the pressure of organized labour, concentrated industries and other like situations; and would not the farmers of Canada generally find themselves out on a limb, as the wheat farmers of the west find themselves to-day? There is some food for thought in these questions for those who are considering a planned economy after this war, and I offer them on the theory and in the hope that they will provoke thought and discussion in this house and elsewhere.
If we are to maintain the economic unity of Canada we must not only be sympathetic to the position of the western wheat farmer;

we must be practical and realistic, and help him. He has made a wonderful contribution to the upbuilding of Canada in the good days of other years; I have always recognized that since I have known anything about the situation. And he will, I feel sure, if given the opportunity, continue to build up and strengthen the economy of this nation. I believe he has the will to do, and I have spoken with many farmers; but in these trying times he must be assisted. The question is one of ways and means. Eastern Canada, industrial Canada, has much to gain by supporting him, and conversely much to lose if he fails. I believe eastern Canada will take the long view and will support him.
In this connection it is very interesting to observe the reaction of eastern Canada to the increased initial price announced by the government. I am going to give only one citation, though I could give many. There are people in this house, some of my hon. friends to the left, and I have heard it from hon. gentlemen opposite as well, who in speaking of the Montreal Gazette commonly credit that journal with being the mouthpiece of the so-called big interests of Canada. In a leading editorial in its issue of March 11, under the caption "More Help for the West" the Gazette had this to say, and I am going to ask hon. gentlemen to listen:
The new measures adopted by the government for the benefit of western agriculture must not be judged from any narrow point of view. If production in the prairie provinces-better balanced due to this and earlier legislation- means a greater national war contribution, that fact alone will go far in justifying steps which under normal conditions might be open to serious criticism. There can be no doubt now that agriculture, not in the Canadian west only but in every part of North America, has an important part to play in feeding allied nations overseas which are no longer in a position to meet their own requirements. This was stressed Monday night by President Roosevelt, VicePresident Wallace and Secretary of Agriculture Claude Wickard, speaking on the anniversary of the national farm programme. Mr. Wickard said then that from accumulated stocks under this programme the United States had been able to send as much as 1,200,000 long tons of food under lend-lease in the period between last spring and February 1, this year, foods without which "it is unlikely that Britain could have withstood the battering which she has received at the hands of the enemy."
And a little further on:
It was axiomatic in peace time that good times in the west meant good times everywhere in Canada. The eastern industrial areas benefited directly from any enlarged western purchasing power and the benefit reached into all business and professional fields.
That does not look like antagonism. It is an evidence of enlightened opinion in the east,

Wheat Board Act
137a
and I commend it to those who are always harping on the alleged attitude of eastern Canada toward western agricultural problems, and who for some ulterior motive endeavour to set east against west and west against east. Let us have an end of that.
It has been emphasized all through western Canada, as well as in the east, that when the Saskatchewan delegation came east there was no compromise which would be acceptable and that what they urged was the minimum with which they would be satisfied and could carry on. It is now quite plain that what is offered is a compromise between two conflicting views. The government was confronted on the one hand with these demands for increased price, and on the other with the necessity of maintaining its own policy of price ceilings, and after much travail and change of policy this compromise emerged. Like most compromises, it is not likely to please anyone-or, at least, very few. It is better than a fixed low price plus a bonus, but it falls short of what is required.
Unquestionably the government had decided on a policy of a fixed price of 70 cents, or thereabouts, plus a bonus. This was indicated by the resolution as first placed on the order paper. But this met with such opposition that it was changed, after what must have been an ultimatum to the government. The change of policy resulted in a compromise.
The principle of maintaining the price ceiling is almost sacred to the Prime Minister and his government. To try to find a formula which would give the wheat growers more money and at the same time not violate that sacred principle has no doubt been difficult, and the result is exactly what was expected by intelligent onlookers. We have a compromise which will not please anybody.
I should like to emphasize the idea that whatever loss is incurred in connection with the raising of the initial price of wheat should be considered a contribution of the Canadian people. The additional difference between 70-cent wheat and a parity price for wheat is a loss which heretofore has been imposed on the wheat producer. That should not be.
If we are to concede the principle of a parity price for wheat, as may be inferred from the speech of the Minister of Agriculture-when the time comes-then it should be contributed by all the people of Canada and not by the producers themselves, or by any limited class of our population, unless, of course, it can be demonstrated-and this is an overriding proviso-that the spread between the cost of the ingredient and labour on the one hand and the price of bread on the other is so great that it may be absorbed 44561-88i
in that quarter. The committee on agriculture, to which the bill is to be referred, should examine those costs and let the people know just what the spread is; and if there is a disparity, it should recommend measures to correct the position.
We shall support the amendment because it is in conformity with the principles we espoused a year ago and which the government rejected. We support it on the theory of war necessity.
This bill and its companion bills 12 and 14 had their first reading on the 6th of March and following days.
On March 5 the governor in council, while parliament was in session and while the bills were in the resolution stage, passed P.C. 1636, under the authority of the War Measures Act, prohibiting the removal of flax from any elevator or mill in Canada without the authority of the wheat board. This was an emergency measure. I do not criticize it, because I deem it a proper use of the power vested in the executive. It had to be done promptly. We can enact for a year, if we wish; and there was no need of haste, because they do not come into effect until August 1 next.
The powers of the wheat board are now to be almost unlimited; and what do we know of the operations of this board? We do know they are a government agency operating a huge business, but the light of day is not let in on their operations. We do know they are piling up a huge liability for this country without any control or say by the people's representatives.
If the house will bear with me I propose for a few moments to analyse in detail some of the operations of the board. The Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, was in the most explicit terms restricted to the buying of wheat from producers only; to pay producers in cash, and to hold the producer's warehouse receipt until an outright sale of the wheat was made. That was fairly simple and very logical. The whole intention of the act was to get the wheat into consumption channels, to the exporters and millers, and it was to do so through established open market trading facilities. It was to sell to real merchandisers, and the wheat was to be sold outright. When a sale was made it was not to be made to a warehouseman. If the board were to hold the producer's wheat beyond fifteen days, the board would pay storage until such time as a sale was made, but once the sale was made the board was to be clear of all further commitments and all storage and other like charges
'Hr. R. B. Hanson.]
were to be received from the merchant who had bought and owned the grain. I refer hon. members in particular to subsection (b) of section 7 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
Let me give the house and the country an example of a buying and selling transaction by the board, as I think all of us understood the function of the board at the time the act was passed. I am told that to operate a country elevator costs about $1,200 a year. This includes operating costs, repairs, upkeep, et cetera. In normal times elevators at country points do not earn storage, and terminal elevators east of lake Superior had, in the past, hardly counted on storage in any substantial way. The terminal elevator earnings were predicated on the handling of grain in large volume. In point of fact, to obtain volume they frequently waived storage charges or fixed them at small rates of one-eighth to one-fourth of a cent per bushel. The country elevator man who receives the grain direct from the farmer, having quite limited possibilities of turnover, is paid a substantial handling charge, I believe of 2! cents per bushel.
As the act was intended to operate, the board's transaction would take this form. It would appoint a local elevator to receive the farmer's wheat on its behalf, pay the farmer the fixed price and hold the warehouse receipt as the agent of the board. If a sale were not made within fifteen days, the board would then become responsible for storage until such time as a sale was made. Once a sale was made, however, the board had nothing further to do with that particular quantity of wheat. The merchant or the miller who bought it was to be responsible for all subsequent charges and had to provide his own price insurance as well. I am sure that the term "price insurance" is well understood by the western members. This merchant provided his price insurance by making a sale of the wheat deliverable at the next futures closing date and at a price sufficiently increased to cover his commission and expenses to that advanced date.
At this point I should like to emphasize that it was just such transactions as these which demonstrated the usefulness of the grain exchange. If anyone wants to elaborate on that, let him read the Stamp report. Skill and resourcefulness on the part of the man on the trading floor was what these merchandisers had to count on in order to make a profit; instead of being in the red, at the time when the grain exchange was on its own, so to speak, and before it became a mere shadow of the Canadian wheat board, as I shall describe it later to be. I am one who believes that the Winnipeg grain exchange served a useful function in normal times, and I still believe that it can

Let me give you now an example of how this board operated under the chairmanship of Mr. Murray, and how it still operates. I ask hon. gentlemen to be good enough to follow me through this intricate transaction. In the first transaction, that is, the buying of the producer's wheat, there is no substantial difference, but it is in the taking of the next step that the act has been violated and the board permitted to operate illegally. I have no doubt about the justification for that statement.

I see by exhibit "B" of this report that the total deficit on the operations for the 1938 crop account was $61,282,329,55. This was the year that the board operated under an 80-cent price and this was the year that the loss was occasioned by statements made simultaneously by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Euler, at the time of the announcement of the 80-cent price. I do not ask hon. members to take my word for it. I shall read what I believe will be accepted as an authoritative commentary-the Economic Journal published in London by the Royal Economic Society and read by economists everywhere. In the June 1939 supplement, Memorandum 79, at page 14 under the caption "The World Wheat Situation", there appears the following: The disparity between exportable surpluses and importers' requirements which became apparent at the beginning of this season was bound to cause severe pressure on prices. But other causes have been at work to produce the precipitate decline which has taken place. Early in August, 1938, the Canadian government fixed a minimum price to farmers of 80 cents 
per bushel, and undertook to pay a subsidy to producers in the western provinces equal to the difference between the minimum price and the market price. At the same time, Mr. Mackenzie King declared that, "Notwithstanding the internal price of 80 cents per bushel, the Canadian wheat board will continue its work of encouraging the use of Canadian wheat, which will at all times be competitive on the world's markets."
He was declaring government policy.
Winnipeg prices were then running at about 85 cents for spot wheat and about 75 cents for October futures. With the announcement of the government's policy the market broke, and futures in spot wheat began to tumble down. By the first week of September Winnipeg spot and futures prices were below 60 cents, the drop in spot thus being greater than in futures. Now the general level of commodity prices declined only very moderately during this period. There was special -weakness in wheat, and among the various wheats special weakness in Canadian wheat, American prices fell by less than half the proportion shown by Canadian. Indeed Canadian No. 1 northern, which is normally at a premium owing to its superior quality, actually fell to a discount under some of the other leading wheats. Winnipeg prices fell below Chicago prices for the first time since in 1937 the United States became once more a net exporter of wheat.
The rapid decline in Canadian prices had clearly been precipitated by the government's announcement. The Canadian government had announced its intention to sell wheat at a loss and without limit. With an exportable surplus of perhaps 250 million bushels in its hands, nearly one-half of world import requirements was to be put on the market under weak selling conditions. Further, the plan was such that producers would be induced to rush delivery and so put a large part of this wheat on the market in the very early months of the season. It was therefore a natural reaction for holders of stocks elsewhere to reduce them and for purchasers to reduce forward commitments to a minimum.
The Canadian plan was not slow to cause reactions in other countries. The United States government quickly decided that it was necessary to ensure the export of 100 million bushels per annum, even, if necessary, by dumping. That this decision was solely a reaction to the Canadian plan is shown by the fact that in 1937-38 the United States had succeeded in exporting more than 100 million bushels and w-as at the time exporting at a considerably greater rate. Before the end of August the premiers' conference in Australia recommended commonwealth and state action to fix an internal price at 4/8 per bushel; and in Argentina the president was empowered to fix such domestic and export prices for the new crop as he considered to be in the interests of the country. Meanwhile some of the minor exporters of the world, notably Roumania, raised their export bounties; while the principal European importers, with the exception of the United Kingdom, imposed further taxes on wheat, or raised its price directly, or, in some cases prohibited imports without special licence. The Canadian government had thus rapidly induced government action on behalf of producers in both exporting and importing countries, and the combined effect of the actions

Wheat Board Act
of all the governments involved was to reduce prices by more than a quarter within the first few weeks of the season.
The decline in prices has hardly induced a comparable change in quantities moving into consumption. It is true that during the first two months shipments were about 20 per cent greater than those of the corresponding period in the previous year, to some extent owing to war fears, though they were still about 15 per cent less than the 1933-37 average. But in the six months October to March shipments were only about 15 per cent greater than in the previous year and 5 per cent less than the 1933-37 average; and this in spite of the fact that there has been some stocking of wheat by European governments, probably on a considerable scale, in order to meet a war situation.

I want the government and the wheat board to give the committee on agriculture and colonization the complete break-down of storage, insurance, interest, brokerage and commissions, and I wish to know on what principle the board operates in paying out brokerage and clearing association charges.
I apologize for taking so much time, but the subject matter is important. As members of parliament we cannot face national problems from any sectional point of view. The marketing of our surplus wheat by availing ourselves of every opportunity to find markets at a price that is remunerative to the farmer is a national problem. I think we must admit that the government's record as a marketer of wheat leaves much to be desired.
The time has come when we should attempt to find a fresh viewpoint. We should examine fearlessly the defects of the present methods, and if a new course-even if a drastic change- is suggested to us by our experience, we should take that course firmly and fearlessly, having regard to the interests of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we have listened with a great deal of interest to all the speeches which have been made this afternoon on these agricultural bills in general, and perhaps the amendment in particular. I think we all recognize that the government are wrestling with many problems, and next to the war agriculture is one of the greatest problems with which they have to wrestle. I think the reason why this wrestling goes on in such a strenuous way is due partly to the fault of the government. It seems to me that the reason for this wrestling is the fact that the government sees this agricultural problem as essentially a money problem. I realize that the moment anyone in this corner suggests that any problem is a money problem, there arises in the minds of many the thought that it is natural for us to say that because we hold to a certain monetary philosophy. I am quite certain that if the government would readjust, or shall I say, reform their money policy, they could then solve their problems, particularly the agricultural problems. I think we have one piece of evidence of this in the minister's own statement on March 10, as reported on page 1211 of Hansard, where he says:
We are taking every last dollar out of the treasury of Canada to deal with these problems which we feel it is safe to take at this present time.
In other words, we can deal with the problem only in so far as the treasury will permit. It never seems to dawn upon the minister or the government that the treasury should' be made to solve the problem instead of the problem awaiting and being entirely dependent upon the treasury. We realize that since the government are pursuing certain policies within the realm of a certain restricted monetary philosophy, they have to go on in their stumbling way from year to year. We realize, therefore that they must be always facing problems instead of solving them.
We realize that the agricultural problem is a problem, and it does seem to me that the problem arises by reason of the fact that agriculture is a primary industry. Somehow or another primary industries never seem to be able to work out an actuarially or scientifically sound price structure for the industry, whatever it may be, while secondary industries, on the other hand, seem to be able to collaborate one with another to work out a scientific price

structure which will guarantee to them a certain profit. Might I illustrate by taking, for example, the automobile industry?
The automotive industry, manufacturing automobiles, tractors, machinery and so forth, calls in its experts, and whether it be a new car model or some feature that has to be put into a certain machine which they are producing, the cost of everything is figured out and goes into the price structure of the article in question. It makes no difference what it is; it may be paint on the automobile or tractor; it may be every little last nut and bolt which are required in the production of a machine; it may be the various taxes which the industry has to pay; it may be depreciation charges, interest on loans, or a hundred and one other things. All these are written into the price structure of that article. The price is arrived at, including dividends and profits, and then a price tag is attached to that particular article. When the consumer comes along, he does not ask, "What will you take for that car?" He always asks, "How much are you asking for it?" There is a price tag on that article and the automotive industry simply says to the consumer, "Take it or leave it. If you do not take it at our price, leave it."
I have never yet heard of a car or tractor or anything of that kind being sold at a bargain price because there was overproduction in the industry.
But what happens when it comes to the primary industry of agriculture? Agriculture has no scientific way of writing into the price of its production all that should go into it. When we talk of cost of production, we must take into account everything that is involved in farming. But that is never done. The farmers have never got together and done it, and it never seems to have dawned on any government or on any official body that they have any need to help agriculture in that matter. The farmer does not say, "I shall have to charge so much for my wheat this year because I find that my buildings need to be painted." But that is exactly what the automobile industry does. The automobile industry writes into the price of its products depreciation on the factory and on all capital equipment. The farmer never does that. Somehow or another he cannot. The very existence of things as they are does not seem to permit him to do it. The agricultural industry does not come to the markets and say, "Here is the price tag on our wheat; here is the price tag on our butter; here is the price tag on our hogs-and the price is so much." The farmer never comes to market and says, "This is my price; take it or leave it." No; world buyers say to the farmer,

"We will give you this price, take it or leave it." Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when the farmer comes to buy, he has to take it or leave it; and when he comes to sell, he has to take it or leave it. That is the position, and I have never yet been able to discover where any government with the responsibilities and problems of agriculture upon its shoulders has ever tried to solve that problem.
