Does it not appear to members of this house and to the people of this country that we have come to a pretty pass when the blessings of Divine Providence have presented us with a problem. I can understand the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) having a problem on his hands when there is a shortage of rubber. I can understand the government having a problem because there might be a shortage of something or another. If our people were starving because there was a shortage of foodstuffs, then I would say indeed that that was a problem. But when we are presented with a problem by reason of the outpouring of blessings from the bountiful hand of the Creator, then I say things have come to a pretty pass.
I would say that the whole fiscal attitude of the government is one of attempting to control within the framework of the present financial system all that we have to do, whether relating to agriculture or to anything else, and I would add, to the war. Of course, we are human beings, not worms; but would the worm starve because the apple was too big? I read somewhere once-I do not know where; it does not matter-that the people of the United States were a nation of playboys. When I hear ministers of governments talking in such a strain as I have mentioned, I must say I believe that as Canadians- we are a nation of screwballs.

I say to this house, through you, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the situation. Not so long ago, maybe in the fall of 1940,
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) had a problem on his hands. Our foreign markets were gone. That was the excuse. It was the excuse the Minister of Agriculture made this afternoon in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch): France has fallen and our market there is gone. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knew that a year or so ago, and knew that the 1940 crop coming on would give a tremendous surplus. He called in, and I think rightly, representatives of the various grain companies and farm organizations of western Canada. They trooped here, and he laid his cards on the table and said to these men: "Now, gentlemen, what have you to suggest?" I think that was the proper thing

to do. What did they suggest? They were unanimous in saying that at least the 1940 wheat crop should be financed. What was the next step? The minister called in the financial representatives-I may be speaking a bit figuratively now-and he said to them, "Gentlemen, how about it?" The gentlemen said "no", doffed their hats and walked out. The Minister of Trade and Commerce turned to the agriculturists and the grain men and said, "There you are, gentlemen. You see. I am sorry, but I cannot do anything. Those who are in charge of our financial system have spoken."
What should he have done? What' should the Prime Minister of this country have done? He should have called in those bankers, those men who are in charge of the money economy of the country, and, putting his cards on the table, he should have said to them: "Gentlemen, this parliament has delegated1 to you the right to issue and control the currency and credit of this nation. You will control it to reflect the physical facts and physical desires of our people or we will go into the banking business." But he did not do that. Oh, no. The men of finance had the last word to say. May I add, is there anything wrong with our having plenty of everything? If the government are pursuing a policy of being restricted and circumscribed by the present financial system, what they are doing in the several bills which they bring down year after year is about the best that we can expect. But I again ask, is there anything wrong about having an abundance of everything-vast stores of grain, of wool-of which commodity we are now becoming very short-of sugar, canned goods, oil or any other commodities? The natural answer is that there cannot be anything wrong with that. Yet, although this is physically possible, merely because the government will not change their financial policy they are met with a problem, and we have to pay people not to produce. This is an alarming condition, and it has come to a pretty pass that we have a government in power which continually harps upon this supposed difficulty, a government which remains within the confines of this restricted system, and which brushes aside as of no account suggested solutions that are offered by other groups.
This afternoon the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) dealt in similar vein with the problem. He spent some time in discussing world carryovers, assuming that because the world has a carryover of grain the Minister of Agriculture is presented with a problem. To me it is the strangest thing that we have to be troubled because we have so much.

speechtext:
The farmers are very patriotic, therefore they must accept as inevitable what the government decides to do, even though it is not enough. Let me ask, will the manufacturing industry do that? As we have pointed out time and again, the manufacturers would not accept a contract unless they could get their 10 per cent profit, even though their wages bill and salaries and directors' fees were written into the cost. Not so with the farmer. We do not contract with the farmer; he has to take it or leave it.
I wish to compliment the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) upon the speech he made this afternoon. In my opinion he has no need to be ashamed of the way in which he has led the official opposition this session. I do not know that I agree with everything he said. Perhaps I am not familiar enough with the details of the business administration of the wheat board. He should be; he was Minister of Trade and Commerce once upon a time. But I agree with him when he deplores the fact that we have a government with no long-range view. Every year they are late in announcing the policy for that year relative to agriculture. What is worse, when the government do come down, in the dying hours of the session, or when the farmer is anxious to get along with his spring work and put in his seed, they make an announcement of policy but they do not bring down their regulations. The result is that farmers do as they think the government want them to do, only to discover afterwards that the regulations have had to be changed, with the consequence that the condition of some of the farmers is not as well at the last as it was at the first.
I wish that we could be certain, when the Minister of Agriculture brings down a bill, that he has the entire picture in his mind. However, if the government is going to muddle through under a system of restriction -and this sort of thing is the best we can expect of them-I suppose we shall have to be satisfied.
I say to the minister that while the details and ramifications of his department may be many, the administration of agriculture in this countiy during the past year has been a shameful record for any government. I live in a diversified constituency, part of which is a rich grain growing area, and I know something of the problems of those farmers. Regulations are passed and then changed. I have a little pamphlet here which I think all hon. members will recognize when I exhibit it. This pamphlet is called, "A Plan to Reduce Wheat Acreage
Wheat Board Act

and Make More Money Available for Necessary War Supplies." It is the same old story of restriction; grow less wheat and help win the war. This pamphlet was printed under the authority of Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, and was intended to outline the regulations governing the wheat acreage reduction plan. Many farmers obtained copies of this booklet, and read them over. Sometimes these things are not simplified enough. I often wonder whether the government employs lawyers to draw up these bills because lawyers know how to confuse the mind by the use of technical and legal terms. However, the farmers got hold of this pamphlet and, after reading it through, thought they understood what the government had decided. The farmers, too, want to win the war, so they decided to grow less wheat. But after this pamphlet was issued, other regulations came out, changing these; then after a while other changes were made, so that the farmer was simply bamboozled and did not know what he was supposed to do.
The same situation exists in regard to administration. This afternoon the hon. member for Acadia referred to the vast number of appointments that had been made, most of which appear to be political appointments. Certainly they were not appointments of men who knew the problems of the farmers. These inspectors have been instructed to go round and tell the farmers certain things. The farmers accept those explanations in good faith, only to find later on that the inspectors had no right to make those statements, or that their statements were wrong, or that in the meantime the regulations were changed. Time after time we have seen that happen, so that when the fall comes round the farmer does not get his cheque, or he does not get as much as he should, or, if he is fortunate, he receives a letter saying this or that was wrong, and he is absolutely confused.
I have an illustration in point; and I think the minister knows all about it. In certain parts of my constituency, as in others, we have what is known as a soil drifting area. The custom among farmers there is not to summer-fallow quite as much as in other districts, because of that soil drifting; they let their land stand idle. When the inspectors came round; the farmers said, "What are we going to do? We usually let this land lie idle, and if we turn it over and summer-fallow it, perhaps it will drift." The inspectors are told to instruct the farmers that if it is their custom to let the soil lie idle and rest for a year, they will receive the bonus just the same. So those farmers carried on as usual and let the land rest. The fall of the year came round, and 
what happened? The minister popped up and said, "Oh, yes; maybe we will pay them, but we will not pay them until the summer-fallow is done." That will be next spring, when the farmer puts in his grain. So the farmer who allowed his land to stand idle is left with his store bill running up, his doctor's bill to pay, and everything else. There he is, as the saying is, left holding the bag.
That is breaking faith with the farmer. I was through a certain part of my constituency before coming to Ottawa; and as late as January, if you please, those farmers had not received their cheques, though they had taken the word of the inspectors or those administering the act. Only to-day I received a letter from the department, in reply to a letter I wrote complaining that a certain man had not received his bonus although six months had elapsed. The reply of the department was, "Well, there is a certain discrepancy in the figures, and therefore we are instructing our supervisor to visit this man." It took them six months before they instructed their supervisor to visit this man, who had to carry on as best he could during the winter. There is something wrong with the administration of the act when this sort of thing happens. I do not like to focus all the blame on certain officials, even though those officials may be political appointees, but one can hardly avoid doing so. Something is wrong somewhere. So I say to the minister: When he brings down a bill or outlines the policy of the government, can we not get a complete picture of it? Cannot regulations be such that the farmers will understand them and, when the time comes, receive payment for the work done? It is not keeping faith with agriculture when the government says to the farmer, "We have a problem, and if you will cooperate we will do so and so." The farmer cooperates; then the government dickers and fiddles over this or that thing and the farmer is'left down at the heels, worn at the cuffs, with store bills, doctors' bills and all sorts of other bills mounting up. I had men come to me with tears in their eyes because they were still waiting for their bonuses, as late as the middle of January. That is not right; it is not fair, and there is something wrong in the minister's department if that sort of thing cannot be remedied.
I see that my time is gone, Mr. Speaker. All I can add is this, that if the government will not act in such a way as to dispose of the problem instead of simply tinkering with it, then I suppose the farmers of this country will have to accept the inevitable and go stumbling on.

Following the statements of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) on second reading of these bills, I covered the situation in a general way, as I thought, and made one or two suggestions. I now desire to state my position with respect to the amendment, and at the outset I should like to say that I do not think it should be considered as a vote of want of confidence. I do not think that should be stressed the way it has been by many of the speakers on the government side. The Minister of Agriculture said it was not a vote of want of confidence in the government, but he stressed that it might be considered a want of confidence in parliament. I cannot go that far. I think this matter should not be considered politically, either, because I believe members of parliament should be free to express ourselves in this house. A speech from this side of the house or from the group in the far comer should not be considered a political speech. I believe a great many hon. members realize their responsibility and are anxious to make some contribution and to offer some help. So far as I am concerned, that is the position I desire to take. I believe, if we all feel we can do something to help solve this problem so as to bring about a state wherein the farmer will receive a better deal or, if you like, receive parity, we ought to do what we can in that direction.
Some pretty warm speeches have been delivered in this debate, even from the government side. We have heard criticism of the government from its supporters, and we have heard replies. I think it may be said, however, that we are all working for a parity. That is a word which has been used often, but I believe it is not well understood even yet. What we want is a situation wherein prices for farm products will compare favourably with the prices the producer has to pay for his implements of production and for the commodities used in production. I might say at this point that if prices could be placed on a parity, and if there is a continuation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which is a form of insurance-and when the measure comes back in final form from the committee I believe it will be worth while-there can be no doubt that we shall get along pretty well.
Since Bill No. 13 has reached its present stage, four orders in council have been passed. This afternoon my leader made reference to these orders in council-and might I add that I believe he ought to be commended for his admirable speech to-day. In his speech he covered the whole situation, going back three
or four years, dealing with the operations of the wheat board and setting out the facts in satisfactory fashion. I believe he has made the position clear, and it is not necessary for me to-night to refer to the operations of the board to any extent. What he has said needs not be repeated.
I contend, as did the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) this afternoon, that these orders in council should be embodied in the bill. They should be part of the bill, and should be offered as legislation. If they are not, then we ought to have a statement from the minister as to how many more orders in council of this kind we may expect. As I have said, four have been passed already, and there is no limit to what we may have. But these four are of such importance that they should be in the bill. I suggest to the minister that he ought to allow the committee to embody some of these orders in council in the bill, so that we may know exactly where we stand.
This afternoon the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) made one or two confessions. He confessed that he now stands for a parity price; that is what he wants. He suggested, too, that Liberal members from the west were capable of reading the riot act, so to speak, to the government, and getting almost what they want. Some of their speeches, however, would indicate that they are not getting what they want. They have all supported the principle of a parity price, an increased price; but I venture to say that within the next hour or so they will not vote for that parity or that increased price. That is my complaint. We are accused of acting politically; we are told that the amendment is a vote of want of confidence; and yet when hon. members opposite come to vote, they will not vote as they have indicated in the speeches they have made.
I believe it is unnecessary for me to make detailed, reference to those speeches. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) endeavoured to answer the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), but I thought his endeavour fell far short of an adequate answer. There are many questions the minister left unsolved, and many charges made by the hon. member for Portage [DOT]la Prairie are still unanswered.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) have honoured me to the extent of referring to some speeches I have made in the house. Before I take my seat to-night I shall make one or two further suggestions, and possibly three or four years from now they may quote me again. There was another hon. member

who referred to me. I will not say who it was. When I came to look through the pages of Hansard I could not find his name, and so I did not think it was necessary to take even thirty-five seconds to answer his thirty-five minutes' speech in which he attacked me.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has made two splendid speeches, and I hope he will follow some of the principles he has enunciated. He of course supports the bill, and does not support the amendment. He has placed on record certain tables to show that the bonus system is the best. My reply to him would be this, that there are 290,000 farmers in the west, and one could prepare a table which would make it appear that 100,000 of them might be better off with the bonus. I might say I had prepared three tables, one of which dealt with half-section farmers, and another with farmers on a section and a half. I could work out those figures to show that so far as the small farms are concerned the bonus might not work out quite as well as it does for the large farms. As I have said, however, that does not prove anything. One could cite dozens of cases, draw tables to show that the bonus would work out better for this man or that man, but that would be no criterion. It does not prove that the bonus does not interfere with the general farming principles or policy of operation in western Canada.
I would ask the government and the board what they will do this fall if the farmers follow out the suggested system of increasing the production of coarse grains. What will they do this fall if we should happen to have

I think I know the farmer pretty well. He is only human, and if he can get 45 cents a bushel for his oats and has a yield of 50 to 100 bushels to the acre- in the northern sections they will have 75 to SO bushels-he will not feel disposed to feed his oats to hogs; he will market them. Whether they are exported to the United States or not, there will be a great flow of oats and barley to the market. I doubt if the United States will take as much as the minister indicates they will. You are going to have your elevator space plugged with coarse grains and wheat.
How about the storage of oats and barley? They command the same rate per bushel and they take practically the same space. I think it will be readily agreed that the farmers will be encouraged to bring their oats to the market rather than to try to store them on the farm under present conditions, unless the government provides for storage or assists in storing on the farm. The small farmer who grows 1,500 or 2,000 bushels additional will have to provide storage unless he is able to take them to market. If the grain exchange continues to function as it is now doing, will it not encourage the marketing of oats and barley and thus encourage the filling up of space that might be required for wheat if we have a large and normal crop?
You can figure it out on a capital investment basis of dollars and cents. Ninety-cent wheat commands 8 cents a year storage. Two bushels of oats would be worth about the same and they would command 16 cents a year storage. Taking the capital investment as far as the elevator is concerned you will see why they will encourage the bringing in of oats and barley. The investment would be much smaller, only about half for wheat, and they would be paid double the storage. This point has not been stressed as yet. I think it is an important one; it is something that will have to be considered.
I suggest that the wheat board should take over everything; it should control storage and other matters to a greater degree than is set out in the orders in council. With government control many of the abuses and injustices to which I have referred before in this house would be eliminated. There are abuses that might have been referred to and enlarged upon the other day by the Minister of Mines

Wheat Board Act
and Resources when he referred to mixing. He said he had had forty years of experience in the grain business and evidently he knows all about mixing. That is one of the first things you find out about when you go into a country elevator. If we had full control, we could do away with some of these injustices.
The first one to which I would refer is undergrading. With this great crop of coarse grains that we expect will be coming to market this fall the government should pay special attention to undergrading. Many oats will grade No. 1 feed instead of 2 C.W. We also have unfair grading of wheat and mixing. The annexes that are being built alongside interior elevators permit of a great deal of mixing. I know what is going to happen. A farmer will bring in No. 1 northern or No. 2 northern wheat. There will be no space for it, and they will take it as No. 3 or No. 4. The same thing will apply to oats. There should be an investigation into this racket that has been perpetrated on the farmers of western Canada in the last three or four seasons in particular. There should be an adjustment of the unjust service charges that are made. Storage charges should not be permitted for storage in boxcars.
At the present time there is only one buyer and only one seller. According to the report for the crop year 1940-41, to which the leader of the opposition referred at great length this afternoon, it will cost this country $60,000,000 to carry this crop next year, taking into account the influx of coarse grains that we expect. As I say, there is only one buyer. I am going to offer a suggestion. I know the hon. member for Rosthern will support me in this, and the hon. member for Dauphin may quote me three or four years from now. I suggest that with the situation as we have it, with this surplus and carryover, with this cost of carrying, parliament should amend the Finance Act so that on the security of the grain in the possession of the board currency could be issued in an adequate volume to finance the board's operations properly, and no interest charges would accrue at any time. We should have the head of the Bank of Canada before the committee in order that we might get some information with respect to the possibilities of doing this. This wheat is practically as good as gold. The government will be in this business for a number of years, and some way should be found to carry it more cheaply, especially when, on the minister's own statement, it is costing us $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 a year.
As was said this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, this bill does not conform to the wheat board act of 1935. Paragraph (b)
of section 3 of that act empowers the board to buy only from the producers of wheat, from no other organization. In the order in council is a clause empowering them to buy wheat from anybody other than producers. We are to start with this new price on August 1. What situation are we going to have? I contend that that price of 90 cents on August 1 is a minimum price and a maximum price. If that is so, then there is no need for the exchange. I do not think there is much need for it at the present time.
I have before me the following report which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of March 14:
Winnipeg wheat futures opened at unchanged price levels in exceedingly dull trading.
They state that there was practically no trading from the first gong until the close. Things appear to be very quiet there now. The exporter cannot raise this 90-cent price, or at least the government has not told us how they can do it. The British cereals import committee buy large quantities, three, four and six months at a time. They set the prices for these amounts at least. Therefore there can be no increase in the price. There will be no demand which would raise the price because under the present set-up nothing but speculation can raise the price. Where are you going to have outside speculation when you have a situation as we have it now, the government taking on 400 million bushels of a surplus and so on?
I ask again: what will the board do with all the oats and barley that will probably come on the market this fall? The Minister of Agriculture has endeavoured to answer this. Apart from the United States market, it would appear that there will be no export to Great Britain. I have before me the parliamentary debates of the British House of Commons of Wednesday, February 4, 1942, and I should like to quote the remarks of Major Lloyd George, as follows:
I am aware of the difficulty which is being experienced in certain areas in Scotland in disposing of feeding oats, and steps have already been taken to relieve the position. A considerable quantity of Scottish feeding oats purchased by the ministry is being moved to localities where they are required for consumption or where storage accommodation is available. I would remind my hon. friend that increased prices have been provided for growers who are able and willing to hold their oats in stack until March or later.
That is the situation over there. Apparently they have more oats than they require.
I have another quotation to the effect that there is going to be an increase in the price of wheat to encourage production in Britain, but I shall not take the time to read it.

I wish now to refer for a moment to one or two speeches which have been made from the other side of the house in an endeavour to show that the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was responsible for the very low price of wheat in 1932. I recall the low price of that period, but I say that the government of that day cannot be blamed for it. I have here the budget speech delivered by the Hon. Charles Dunning on May 1, 1930. Some hon. members may have seen this little summary of the Dunning budget, containing his picture. In that May day budget speech he reported that our sales of export wheat were down $243,000,000 and that our sales of export flour were down $20,000,000 from the previous year. He also stated that the price of No. 1 northern at Fort William had dropped in 1929-30 from $1.55 to 82 cents. Who was responsible for that drop? If the Liberal government will take the responsibility for the drop in 1929-30, when wheat went down 73 cents a bushel, I would be willing for the Bennett government to take the responsibility for the drop from 80 to 40 cents in the first two years it was in office.
I shall not deal further with the question of parity prices. That is nothing new because the principle was adopted in the Conservative party platform prior to the last election. It was adopted in January, 1940. I have a copy of the speech made by the Hon. Robert Manion in western Canada in which he said that he was in favour of a fair parity price for the farmer and that if his party were returned to power he would provide for storage on the farm and set a fair price comparable with the price the British farmer received. So a parity price is nothing new. It was part of the policy of the Conservative party at that time.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his address the other night made several splendid suggestions which I trust the minister will be prepared to have considered and adopted when this measure goes before the committee.

I should like to say a word about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We were twitted by the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) because we were not debating it. It had gone to a committee. But let me say that right from the outset we not only supported the principle of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act but advocated a broadening of its provisions. We have always hoped that this measure would develop into a real form of crop insurance, and that that crop insurance would be, like other forms of insurance, on an individual basis. We should like to have seen the Prairie Farm Assistance Act further extended, not restricted, this year.
Some attempt has been made in this house to confuse the entire issue by talking about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and wheat prices at the same time. The two things are entirely different. The price of wheat is the problem of a depressed industry; the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is the problem of a distressed area, two different problems altogether, which should be considered distinctly and apart. The wheat price should be a reasonable price,

Wheat Board Act

as a matter of justice to a depressed industry, depressed because of uncontrollable conditions as far as the farmer is concerned-by war now, and in past days by government policy, such as the imposition of tariffs, which made him sell his produce in the open free market of the world and buy his supplies in a completely protected and closed market. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act deals with a depressed area, due to crop failure, drought, grasshoppers and the other plagues with which the western producer has been cursed.
Again, may I say, to some extent this was caused by faulty national policies; land settlement policies, organized by railways and governments, opening up land which never should have been opened to the plough, and of course aggravated by low prices in the few good crop years that we experienced. I am not going into that to-night. I am just going to say that so long as we fail to face the problem of the marginal and sub-marginal lands

of which there is not as great an area as many people think-and deal with it, perhaps in some instances by larger irrigation policies than were instituted under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act with some success, or by resettlement so that the people now occupying those lands may be humanely moved to places where they can make a living, so long must we continue to use and expand the present crop failure bonus system. As I have said, I should like to see it so expanded that payments would be on the basis of the individual farm.
Thus the two problems, the problem of the distressed industry and the problem of the depressed area, are distinct. The first, the distressed industry, can be dealt with under a decent parity price. This is realized by a very large number of people in western Canada.
In Saskatchewan alone, approximately 185,000 people signed the petition in favour of an initial payment of $1, looking to parity prices in the future. These 185,000 contributed their mites to send more than 400 representative farmers to meet this government and members of this house. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that when I saw those people here I was proud of them. A finer group of men, the railways told us, had never been transported across Canada; and their presentation here was something that did both them and the people who sent them the greatest credit.
They want $1 as an initial payment. That does not approach the parity price. It does not give them, according to the records of our own experimental farms and our universities, even the cost of production. Then they hope that during the year improved conditions may enable payments to be made to bring the final

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 be granted to his majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1943, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(e) promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
(d) the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. 1931, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $2,000,000,000 as may be required for the purpose of defraying such expenses or making such advances or loans, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditure under the war appropriation acts of 1939 (second session), 1940, 1941 and 1942.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon (Mr. Vien) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
This is an important resolution, and at this stage I should like to make a brief statement with respect to the subject matter. There are so many other matters that must be advanced before the Easter recess that it is not my expectation that we shall be able to debate this resolution at all, or at least to any extent, before the Easter adjournment, but it is important for the purposes of interim supply that it be placed before the committee of the whole as is being done to-night. If the committee thinks fit, I suggest that I make a statement on the resolution and that then the committee report progress and we go on to some other measure which it is important should be introduced and dealt with before the Easter recess. The debate on this resolution in committee of the whole will, I assume, take days and perhaps weeks, because this is the occasion when the members of the House of Commons have their opportunity of asking the government what disposition was made of the money that was voted last year, why we require so much money this year, and what is to be done with the money that is to be voted. It is not a matter which I would expect to be dealt with quickly. My suggestion is, if I may repeat, that I make a statement on the subject tonight. Then someone might move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and we could go on with other financial matters.
This resolution seeks permission to introduce a measure which will provide the major appropriation for our war expenditures during the new fiscal year which begins on April 1. If the resolution passes, it will be followed by a bill which, when enacted, will become the War Appropriation Act, 1942. The bill will be in substantially the same form as the appropriation acts of 1939, 1940 and 1941, except that the amount requested will be vastly' greater, reflecting the ever-growing scale of Canada's war effort. But even the $2,000,000,000 requested by this resolution will fall far short of representing the total sum which will be required during the next fiscal year to finance Canada's war expenditures.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) explained to the house some weeks ago, our total war expenditures for next year are estimated at approximately $3,000,000,000, roughly about six times the total expenditures of this government in the pre-war years. Hon. members may ask how the remaining $1,000,000,000 will be provided1. As the speech from the throne indicated, it is our intention to ask parliament to approve the making of a free and unconditional gift of $1,000,000,000 worth of foodstuffs, raw materials, munitions and

War Appropriation
other war supplies, to the United Kingdom. In other words, instead of the indirect assistance to Britain, which we have been giving in the past, in order to enable her to finance her enormous purchases in Canada, we propose in future to provide these war supplies to Britain as a direct part of Canada's war effort, up to the amount of $1,000,000,000. It is therefore my intention to move later-I hope to-morrow -a companion resolution now on the order paper, which will seek authority to introduce another appropriation bill, which will be called the War Appropriation (United Kingdom financing) bill. This latter bill will provide, among other things, for an appropriation of $1,000,000,000 for this purpose.
It is true that the appropriations to be authorized by this second measure will not relate exclusively to the fiscal year 1942-43. It will provide continuing statutory authority not related to any one fiscal year. It is my hope that it will be passed promptly and that the appropriation it will provide will become operative during the present fiscal year and will cover expenditures incurred during, say the present month as well as during the remaining months of 1942 and for some time in 1943.
When the War Appropriation (United Kingdom financing) bill is before the house I shall attempt to explain more fully how the $1,000,000,000 appropriation is to be divided between this year and next year. I thought, however, it was necessary for me at this time to make this brief reference in order that the house might understand why we are asking at this time, in the present resolution, for only $2,000,000,000, although we have estimated that our war expenditures will run to about $3,000,000,000 during the coming fiscal year.
If I may now return to the resolution which I have moved, I would point out that the main war appropriation bill which the resolution precedes will, as last year, contain three essential features. First, it will ask for a vote of credit for war purposes, but this time, as I have said, for $2,000,000,000. Second, it will ask for a grant of borrowing authority; in other words, the bill, if passed, will enable the government to borrow funds to pay for any of the expenditures covered by the vote of credit if such borrowings are proved to be necessary. Third, as was the case with last year's bill, the new bill will confer power on the government to act as the agent of any British or allied government and, in this capacity, to incur temporarily obligations or costs which are recoverable from the government concerned. One of the few changes in
this year's bill is to extend this power to cover obligations or costs temporarily incurred by a crown corporation such as War Supplies Limited, while acting as agent of the British or an allied government.
The first of these three features, namely the grant or vote of credit, is, of course, the most important aspect of the bill. To enable the house to discuss the magnitude of the vote requested, I shall first give some data and estimates as to our direct war expenditures during the current fiscal year. Hon. members will recall that when I spoke on the corresponding resolution of last year I said that the government had decided to ask parliament for an initial war appropriation of $1,300,000,000, although the war programme, as then outlined, would involve, according to the estimates of the departments, a total estimated expenditure in excess of that sum by perhaps $150,000 000. I explained some of the difficulties involved in making any advance precise estimates or rather forecasts of the probable cost of a full year's war effort, and I stated that if the departmental estimates were in fact realized, it would be necessary to come back to parliament for' a supplementary appropriation toward the end of the fiscal year.
As every one knows, the monthly expenditures on war have been rising rapidly, and I expect that within a few days I shall have to introduce a supplementary appropriation for the current fiscal year for an amount of probably $135,000,000 to carry us through to the end of this month and to take care of outlays during April relating to expenditures made during the present fiscal year ending this month.
The latest estimate, which was made some days ago, and is still subject to revision, is that total direct war expenditures for the current year will reach about $1,431,000,000. This total may be broken down approximately as follows:

This amount, it will be noted, is very close to the total of the estimates made by the departments last spring. As the house may recall, it contrasts with total direct war
War Appropriation

expenditures of $778,000,000 (including $26,000,000 of advances and loans charged to active assets) for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, and with total war expenditures of $118,000,000 in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1940.
The estimate I have just given of our war expenditures for the current fiscal year does not, of course, include the indirect assistance which we have given to the United Kingdom, and concerning which I expect to give the figures when I am dealing with the companion resolution now on the order paper.
But even excluding this substantial indirect assistance, the total represents an amount to be spent on a single year's war effort which to all of us in 1939 would have seemed incredible. For the new fiscal year, the corresponding figure for what has in the past been called our direct war effort will be nearly 50 per cent larger. As last year, we have aimed at a war programme which will represent the country's utmost capacity, the maximum which we can carry out with the physical and economic resources at our disposal. That capacity, it must be remembered, increases each year the war goes on, as existing plants are expanded and new plants are constructed to produce war equipment and supplies, as labour is trained and administrative skills are developed, as civilian expenditures are more and more restricted, and as our economy generally is more and more converted into a war economy.
I am free to say that the estimates submitted by the service departments, the Department of Munitions and Supply, and the various other departments engaged in war work, total up to a higher figure than the $2,000,000,000 which we have decided to ask parliament to authorize at this time. I need not, however, labour again the great difficulties of making precise forecasts so far in advance of actual expenditures, and particularly in a time as uncertain as the present; and of course it is always possible to come back to parliament for a supplementary appropriation if before the end of the new fiscal year it should prove that the actual expenditures are likely to exceed the vote for which we are now asking.

Every hon. member will admit that the discussion of this resolution is much more important than any debate or discussion on the plebiscite and, in my humble view, it should have come before the house much earlier, so that hon. members would have had an opportunity to discuss the whole matter.
This is not a time to make speeches and homilies; it is a question of knowing how money will be spent, and that is all. Here we are facing again the question of ministerial responsibility. At times we hear ministers say, "We have assumed a tremendous responsibility." I understand that in a time of war it is no fun, and the ministers have to make decisions. But those decisions are not the ministerial responsibility. Ministerial responsibility is the rendering of public accounts to the representatives of the people assembled in the House of Commons of Canada, whether they sit in the house or in committee.
Last year I remember well that I mentioned the way in which public accounts were rendered, and pointed out that I was scandalized by the condition of affairs. I could not conceive why it should be that the larger the expenditure, the tinier would be the public account, and I made representations to that effect. The accounts are rendered by the auditor general, and we do not find in them any items of a less amount than $5,000.

speechtext: I think it is $35,000 now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps; that is much worse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is why I said it was worse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is much worse. There is not a single elector in Canada who is not entitled to full information concerning the rendering of public accounts.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Sometimes we hear complaints about the number of questions asked in the house by hon. members about the salaries paid to Mr. So-and-so, or the travelling expenses of Mr. So-and-so, or the living allowance of Mr. So-and-so, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. In former years it was easy to look into the public accounts, which were certified by an officer of the crown receiving $15,000 a year, who could be discharged only by joint vote of the Senate and the House of Commons. Those accounts were complete. Then, if an elector, no matter how humble, came to his member to obtain some information about this man, that man or the other man, after having a glance over the public accounts the member was in a position to inform his constituent without having to ask the government a question during a session.
I have had a glance at the Orders of the Day and Votes and Proceedings, and I have seen the numerous questions asked by my colleagues for information which was available in former years without making any request. Is it because we are at war that we have completely lost responsible government-the responsible government for which our ancestors in this country fought? Have we lost the responsible government for which William Lyon Mackenzie, the grandfather of my chief, the Prime Minister, suffered so much? We have statues all round this building, and I
War Appropriation

would draw the attention of hon. members particular!}' to the monument commemorating Lafontaine and Baldwin, the men who succeeded in obtaining responsible government for Canada.
Not only have we lost responsible government, but we have lost even the notion of responsible government. We are now asked to swallow a piece of legislation referring to the expenditure of the astronomical sum of $2,000,000,000. We are asked1 to spend it like a drop of water-not a glass of water, just a drop. It is pretty hard for us to do that, because the constituents of each hon. member, whether on this side of the house or on that side, will have their right not only to inquire of their members about public accounts, but to ask those members in their own offices, or where they may receive the people of their constituency, "Sir, I am coming to you for information. Will you please tell me how much has been spent for-" some work, or possibly a salary, or some other kind of expenditure. Will those constituents be satisfied if the member answers: "Wait until the next session, and if we have an opportunity before adjournment we shall try to get the information for you."
No; it is not a matter of making speeches; it is a matter of getting accurate and complete information. The discussion will be longer just because of the fact that the public accounts are shapeless. There is not a province in Canada, not a city, not a township, not a village, no matter how small, where public accounts like these would be accepted, where they would satisfy those who have the responsibility of government. I am not talking in a grouchy or harping way; I am saying this because I feel it is my public duty. I am ready to support the government to the limit, but I do not want this house to lose rights for which our ancestors paid so dearly.
When I refer to the house, I do not mean only when Mr. Speaker is in the chair; I am referring also to when we sit in committee of the whole. We should follow the great example and traditions at Westminster. They are at war in England just as we are. They do not feel that being at war makes it impossible to check expenditures. The committee of national economy sits daily under the roof of Westminster and every expenditure is checked. There is public control through the members of parliament-they have the House of Lords and we have the Senate-over every expenditure, no matter how small. Last year I was promised solemnly-the house was promised that there would be an improvement in the public accounts. But nothing has been
(Mr. Pouliot.j
done; they are worse than before. I do not speak as a bad Liberal; I speak as one who is a Liberal at heart.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You are speaking a lot of good sense to-night.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would listen to me all the time, he would say that quite often. We must follow what has been done at Westminster during the long centuries since magna charta. There has been ministerial responsibility for the rendering of complete accounts for each expenditure. That is the British tradition. It is not sufficient for anyone to wrap himself in the British flag and say that he is a good British citizen. The flag represents a great past and great ideals, but there is something important that should never be forgotten. I refer to the traditions which have been followed closely during the centuries, the traditions of true democracy. We must follow these real British traditions in this house if we are to remain a British House of Commons.
I do not intend to say much more to-night because I have said enough. I have expressed my very deep disappointment and r, for one, will not tolerate such legislation pasoing in a hurry. We shall have to take our time. I am ready to sacrifice the Easter adjournment and stay here in Ottawa in order to scrutinize these expenditures to the last cent. I have made other sacrifices and I am ready to make this one. I might take a Sunday in order to see my electors, but I am ready to sit here every day in the week except Sunday and work conscientiously as a member of parliament in order to keep the confidence of my people.
If the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) wishes to go to Vancouver, he can stay with us all week, take an aeroplane at night, spend the afternoon in Vancouver and be back with us the day after. But I am sure that he is ready to make the same sacrifice as I am, and I am sure that, all other hon. members are ready to do the same. Let us not be afraid to talk British common sense in times of war as well as in times of peace. The promise to which I have referred was made to the whole house because it was given at three o'clock on the orders of the day by no less a person than the right hon. the Prime Minister, my leader. That promise should not be forgotten. Moreover, that promise will be kept. I suggest that the public accounts which are unsatisfactory should be republished in as complete a form as they were during the last war. They are simply shapeless now. The smallest municipal council, the smallest school commission, would not

War Appropriation
accept accounts like that. How is it that we as members of parliament, representing 245 constituencies-244 now-should be expected to accept such shapeless accounts?
Let us not be afraid to use plain language to express our thoughts. My -language to-night has not been private; it has not even been feeble. I believe I have spoken clearly enough to be understood by everyone. This is no joke. We are ready to go the limit to support the government, but this passes the limit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is beyond the limit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is beyond the limit; the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) is absolutely right. This matter is serious. The victory -loan campaign is over and the loan has been oversubscribed, so it cannot be said that we would be handicapping its success by discussing these questions. Every one did his share to make the loan a success. As I told my constituents-I want Hansard to translate that as "eleeteurs"-on previous occasions, it was the right thing to subscribe to the victory loan, but I was coming to Ottawa to try to check expenditures so that there would be no waste.
What I said to my people in my constituency-and I want Hansard to translate the word "constituency" by "comte"-I repeat now because I have no two ways of expressing myself, one way in the House of Commons and a different way in Temiscouata. I use the same language in both places and it pays in the long run. I hope that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will have an opportunity to think over this matter and, as night sometimes brings good counsel, that he may change his opinion. There might be an amicable, friendly discussion in the best possible spirit. But the most important thing is not the expression of views, however respectable they may be, by any member of parliament in this house. The most important thing is to know what is going on and how the money is spent.

speechtext: You cannot find that out in the public accounts to-day.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We shall have to get it from the committee in due course.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If the proposal made by the Minister of Finance is carried out, the effect will be that there will be no discussion of the war effort across the floor of this house until this house meets again on April 20. To me it is almost inconceivable that the house would agree to a step of that kind being taken. The resolution which is before us to-night, and which has come up although we were told it would not come up, gives us the
one chance of the whole session to discuss Canada's war effort thoroughly. There is no chance to do that on the bill which follows the resolution. The chance is on the resolution itself, and I for one do not propose to agree, if unanimous agreement is required, to any course that will result in deferring all the discussion of Canada's war effort until after April 20. We have been here already for nearly two months, and in that time there has been no real opportunity at all to discuss-Canada's war effort. With the enemy threatening us on our east coast and on our west coast this house has seen fit to talk for four weeks on the speech from the throne, then for several weeks on the plebiscite, then for many more days on wheat, as if there were no war raging in the world at all. That is setting a terrible example to the people of Canada. How can we ever expect to have our people put their backs into this war when this house carries on in that way? Then to have the government make this proposal to-night I think is an insult to the Canadian people. I suggest, I demand, that every minute from now until this house adjourns on the 27th of March be spent in discussing the war effort of this nation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to
protest against this way of doing business. His majesty's forces are represented in this house by three ministers, one for the army, one for the navy, and one for the air force, and not one of these ministers is here to-night. I protest against voting $2,000,000,000 at 10 o'clock to-night. We spent in 1896 $36,000,000 for the total maintenance charges of Canada. Where are we in this war? Nobody knows where we are. We have nothing in the Pacific at all.
I say to the government, you have let Australia down. Before the war started you were dependent on pacifists. This resolution speaks for itself; but before the war, you not only threw away defence, but threw away your friends. The Minister of Finance now brings down a resolution-
-that sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 be granted to his majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1943.
All that $2,000,000,000 will not amount to 50 cents in beating Hitler. You let Australia down. You threw Australia to the wolves at the imperial conference in 1937 when Australia asked this dominion to give a large grant to the Singapore base, which would have resulted in safeguarding British Columbia and the Pacific. But this government at that conference refused to have anything to do with the
War Appropriation

Singapore base, and refused to adopt the Jellieoe report which would have given us adequate protection in the Pacific. You had a navy of three or four cruisers and a destroyer, boats which, added up, amounted to 9,240 tons, about the size of a good 10,000-ton tramp steamer to protect us in the Pacific. When we saw the war coming; when Hitler had invaded Czechoslovakia, when his armies had crossed the Rhine, which Mr. Baldwin said was our first line of defence, this government and hon. gentlemen opposite refused at that colonial conference of 1937 to go into an empire shipping scheme. They were told at that conference by New Zealand and Australia what the disasters might be to this dominion from the Pacific, and they refused to do a thing. They said: "We have no commitments, parliament must decide."
When you look -at the text of this resolution for $2,000,000,000, you see that it is for "the security, defence ... of Canada." What security or defence have we had in the past from a similar vote since the war broke out?
